heroLead: Loco Hills is one of the older names in Eddy County oil, a field that's been producing in one form or another since the 1920s.
intro: This one's a genuinely historic field. Loco Hills was developed early, went through waterflood in the mid-20th century like a lot of shallow Permian fields did, and has kept producing at a modest rate ever since. If your family's minerals here have been in the same hands for generations, that fits the pattern we see.

sections.heading: What long-lived production means for value
paragraphs: A field that's been producing for a century tends to be well understood, decline curves are established, workover history is documented, and there's rarely a surprise waiting in the data. That predictability is actually useful when we're putting together an offer, we're not guessing at how a Loco Hills well behaves over time.

sections.heading: Old paperwork, older assignments
paragraphs: Interests this old have often been assigned, split, and re-recorded multiple times, sometimes with handwritten instruments from decades back. We're comfortable working through that kind of chain of title, it just takes a careful read of the Eddy County Clerk's older recorded volumes.

sections.heading: Waterflood economics, in plain terms
paragraphs: A field on waterflood produces at a steadier, more predictable rate than a fresh horizontal well, but the total volume recovered over time is generally lower than what modern completions achieve. That trade-off is worth understanding if you're weighing whether to sell now or keep collecting royalty from a well like this for years to come.

faqs.question: How old is production at Loco Hills?
faqs.answer: The field dates back to the 1920s and has produced through multiple phases of development including mid-century waterflooding. It's one of the older continuously producing areas in Eddy County.

faqs.question: My deed is handwritten and decades old. Can you still work with it?
faqs.answer: Yes, older handwritten and re-recorded instruments are common on Loco Hills tracts, and we're used to tracing chain of title through the county clerk's older recorded volumes.

faqs.question: Is a century-old field still worth selling minerals in?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Long production histories give us a well-understood decline curve to price against, which can make valuation more straightforward than a brand-new well with no track record yet.

faqs.question: Should I hold onto a waterflood royalty or sell it now?
faqs.answer: That depends on your personal timeline and risk tolerance. Waterflood production tends to be steady but gradually declining, so it's worth weighing years of smaller checks against a lump sum today. We'll show you the numbers either way.
